chapter_theme: The battle over Gandharvadattai ends: Padumukan's elephant and arrows and Civakan's conch rout the envious kings, who take him for Murugan and scatter, and the narrator declares that victory goes to the virtuous mind. Civakan brings the bride home, the wounded are treated and rewarded, he expiates the sin of the battlefield by a golden image of the Jina, a festival and gifts and worship at the Tirthan's feet, and the stores for the great wedding pile up, led by Nandagon's pots of milk, curd and ghee.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, who has won Gandharvadattai at the vina
Civakan's friend, who fights from an elephant and tends the wounded
Civakan's companions, who fight beside him
the kings who came seeking the princess and make war over her
the Vidyadhara kings who watch and cheer Civakan's fight
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, won by Civakan at the vina, now his bride
the women who give the wounded ghee food as medicine
the herd chief, keeper of the king's herds, who brings milk, curd and ghee for the wedding

805.reading: As rice cooked with ghee grows sweeter when nectar from the sea is added, the warriors, seeing the young lord's strong chariot rolling over the bodies of his foes, carry the spears that have split their chests and fight the harder.
805.event: Civakan's chariot drives over the enemy dead and his men, though wounded by spears, fight on more fiercely.
805.nuance: The simile makes the sight of the leader's chariot a seasoning: it does not change the fight but sharpens what the warriors already have. Whether மைந்தர் are Civakan's men or the enemy's is not stated; the sense of growing valour points to his own side.

806.reading: Padumukan drives forward a roaring elephant in musth, like the fire at the end of an age, which with its crescent tusks, strong trunk and hind legs kills in the battle for the maiden as if refusing to give her to others.
806.event: Padumukan sends his war elephant into the battle fought over the princess, and it kills the enemy.
806.nuance: குமரிப் போர் names the war for what it is, a fight over a girl; the elephant is made to fight as if it too were a suitor who will not yield her (கொடாம் பிறர்க்கு).

807.reading: Felling kings with its tusks, lashing with its tail, crushing chariots with its trunk, trampling leaping horses under its feet and burning foes to ash with the fire of its eyes, the elephant makes blood flow while demons sing and dance, and the rider angrily takes up his strong bow.
807.event: The war elephant destroys kings, chariots and horses, and its rider takes up his bow.
807.nuance: The rider who takes the bow is not named; continuing from 806 he is read here as Padumukan, though the bow-work that follows could belong to Civakan. Line 3 (கண்ணுட் டீயாற சுட்டு) looks corrupt for கண்ணுள் தீயால் சுட்டு.

808.reading: He took his bow, fitted the arrows, the bow bent in a circle, and seeing chariots, elephants' heads, the flanks of bee-swarmed horses and the fierce kings, he poured a rain of arrows that fell among them all.
808.event: The archer looses a shower of arrows on the chariots, elephants, horses and kings.
808.nuance: The verse runs on the verbs கொண்டான், தொடுத்தான், கண்டான், சொரிந்தான், so that the shooting is told at the speed of the act; it picks up கொண்டான் from the end of 807.

809.reading: Laughing, he says that the herds of gold-caparisoned elephants, the masses of red-gold chariots and the sea-flood of the army are nothing but the leftovers of the arrows that travel from the lord's bow, and that there are no kings of gold ornament left at all.
809.event: The archer mocks the enemy, saying their whole army is only what the lord's arrows have left.
809.nuance: நம்பன் is used of Civakan in 811; if the laughing speaker is his friend, he credits the rout to Civakan's bow even while he fights. The speaker is not named, and the verse could also be the narrator's report of the archer's taunt.

810.reading: 'One man alone, one bow alone, on one elephant, and he did not even notice the spear that went into his mountain chest: will kings still fight?' said one, and they unstrung their bows, turned back their elephants and put up their swords.
810.event: Struck by the lone fighter's disregard of a spear wound, the hostile kings give up the fight and turn back.
810.nuance: The one who speaks is unnamed; the plural verbs that follow (மடக்கியிட்டார், மீட்டார்) make it a king among the attackers whose words turn the rest. வாட்படை வாங்கிக் கொண்டார் can mean they drew their swords or withdrew them; the unstrung bows favour withdrawal.

811.reading: When the lord set to his mouth a conch shaped like the right-whorled conch that red-eyed Mal sounds, and blew it, all the garlanded kings faltered and their eyes dimmed, like a great herd of elephants wailing at the roar of a fierce lion.
811.event: Civakan blows his conch and the enemy kings lose heart.
811.nuance: The conch is likened to Vishnu's, so the hero's blast borrows the god's; the verse wins the battle by sound rather than by a blow.

812.reading: Shaken like the sea when the one of the wheel churned it with the serpent wound round the mountain, the kings cried that the broad-chested one's chariot was the peacock and he was Murugan himself, and broke so that no two of them stayed together.
812.event: Taking Civakan for Murugan on his peacock, the hostile kings scatter in panic.
812.nuance: Two gods are borrowed in one verse: Vishnu churning the sea for the kings' turmoil, Murugan for the hero they think they see. The kings' cry is a mistake born of fear, not the poet's claim that Civakan is divine.

813.reading: Like a roaring fire that grazes through a forest of dry trees, the prince's companions of clear worth roared like Death and scattered arrows, and the sea-like army of the drunk-with-pride kings broke as a shining hill of salt crumbles in a flood.
813.event: Civakan's companions shower arrows and the kings' great army breaks up.
813.nuance: The salt hill dissolving in water is an image of a mass that has no cohesion of its own: the kings' sea of soldiers is large but melts at the first flood.

814.reading: Do not ask whether a small band could beat kings with great armies and come away unharmed: a lion with close-set teeth kills a great herd of elephants, and a single tiger attacks a herd of deer.

claims.claim: a single strong one can rout a great host, as one lion scatters a herd of elephants

814.nuance: The narrator turns to the listener (என்ன வேண்டா) to answer a doubt about the story's plausibility; the answer is from nature, and 815 then gives a moral cause as well.

815.reading: Those who do good are missed by the sword and do not fall, and for those who do evil no weapon finds its mark; those great in virtue win even if they throw a betel leaf, for it becomes a spear, and there is no victory for those in whose minds evil has made its home.

claims.claim: weapons do not fell those who do good, and those who do evil cannot strike home
victory belongs to the virtuous and never to those whose minds harbour evil

815.nuance: வெற்றிலை (betel leaf) puns on வெற்று இலை, a bare leaf: the weakest missile becomes a spear in a good man's hand. The verse does not say the virtuous never fight; it says the outcome of their fighting is decided by the state of the mind.

816.reading: The kings who had waged a war of envy over the eyes of the girl with earrings vanished faster than lightning in a cloud; the Vidyadhara kings praised the hard fighting of the one like a lion in its cave and shouted, and the old city of festive streets overflowed with joy.
816.event: The hostile kings flee, the Vidyadhara kings cheer Civakan's fight, and the city rejoices.
816.nuance: கோணைப் போர் is a crooked or spiteful war; the poet names the kings' cause as envy over a girl's eyes, not a claim of right.

817.reading: Having seen the battlefield the world praises, Civakan, his chest scored with red furrows ploughed by the white tusks of the enemy war elephants, and surrounded by his companions, took the girl of fortune's grace and bound breasts into his house.
817.event: Civakan, wounded, leads Gandharvadattai into his house with his companions around him.
817.nuance: The tusk wounds are drawn as plough furrows (சால்) on his chest, so that the bridegroom enters the house bearing a field of war on his body.

818.reading: Some were laid in troughs of ghee, some were stretched in ghee tubs, some had the spearheads sought out where they had entered and cut out with iron, some shed on the earth the tears that ran with their eye-black, some were given purses of coin, and some were given many ornaments.
818.event: The wounded are treated with ghee and surgery, and rewarded with money and ornaments.
818.nuance: The passive refrain (பட்டார்) lists the wounded only by what is done to them; healing and reward stand in one list, as if both were care owed to the fighters. Line 3 may describe the pain of the surgery or mourning for the dead; the verse does not say.

819.reading: For those whose whole bodies were holed with wounds like the hollows of an old tree, the good women set balls of food with ghee, saying 'this is medicine', and Padumukan laid ghee-soaked cloths close on their chests and urged them off to beds of soft fur.
819.event: Padumukan and the women tend the wounded with ghee food and dressings and send them to rest.
819.nuance: பதுமுகன் பாவை மார்பின் is hard to construe; பாவை may go with the women rather than with Padumukan, and the verse's single verb (நூக்கினான்) is his.

820.reading: The lord whose chest gleams with garland and single chain made an image of the Holy One in green gold of the earth, held a festival through the town, gave wealth gladly, and with lament put away the sin of the battlefield.
820.event: Civakan has a golden image of the Jina made, holds a festival and gives gifts to expiate the killing in battle.

claims.claim: killing in battle, even a just one, leaves a sin that worship, festival and giving can put away

820.nuance: The epic does not treat the victory as sinless because it was defensive: போர்கெழு களத்துப் பாவம் is named outright, and it is removed with புலம்பு, grief, not only with rite. பண்ணவன் is the Jina as the work's own Lord.

821.reading: He of the long right-whorled-marked hand stretched out to protect the world took the remnant from the feet of the Tirthan who removes all sins committed, bowed, worshipped and praised, and took the water of the right-whorled conch made of flawless gem.
821.event: Civakan worships at the Tirthankara's feet, receives the offering's remnant and takes the water from the jewelled conch.

claims.claim: the feet of the Tirthankara remove all sins one has done

821.nuance: தீர்த்திடும் தீர்த்தன் puns on the Tirthan as the one who removes (தீர்). The claim of sin removed at the Jina's feet sits beside the work's teaching elsewhere (375) that deeds wear away on the path of knowledge. The word read as கூலித் in line 2 is doubtful.

822.reading: What is now told is the great wedding of the girl like a golden branch, round whose breasts, like a jewel casket set with dark gems and red rays, fine gems swing.
822.nuance: A short verse in a new metre opens the wedding section; the narrator announces the subject (பேசுகின்றதே) rather than telling an act.

823.reading: The guardian of the king's herds, lord of the shining spear, brought four hundred thousand pots filled fair with fine curd, milk and ghee, so that the town was amazed at the wedding feast.
823.event: Nandagon brings four hundred thousand pots of curd, milk and ghee for Civakan's wedding.
823.nuance: வேள்வி here is the wedding as a feast, not a Vedic sacrifice. The herd chief is not named; கோன் தொறுக் காவலன் fits Nandagon, keeper of the king's herds.

824.reading: On one side carts of white long-grained paddy rice, carts of countless sugar, carts of split pulses and carts of salt from sea-water stood crowded.

825.reading: On another side, jackfruits heavy as drums on their branches, bananas and mangoes where the bees hum, tubers and vegetables of every kind carried by crowds left no room to stand.

826.reading: On another side, bunches of tender areca green as emerald, ripe areca hung to ripen, and bundles of tender betel leaf were poured out like a sea with no room left.
826.nuance: The refrain ஒர்பால் (on one side) in 824 to 827 builds the wedding stores as a panorama, one heap per verse.

827.reading: On another side, crowds carrying loads of fragrant flowers, champak, tamanakam, tamala, jasmine, cool kazhuneer, kuvalai and lotus, with bees humming over them, made a splendid show.

links.note: The Vidyadhara king said he would not give his daughter even if kings with sea-like armies fell at his feet and begged; here the kings who fought for her lose their sea-like army, which breaks like a salt hill in flood.
links.teaches: The father's refusal was spoken before any war, and the battle turns his figure of speech into fact: the same sea of soldiers he would not bow to is now the thing that dissolves.

links.note: Nandagon promised Civakan to fill the underworld with ghee of red cows, sweet milk and thick curd; here the keeper of the herds brings four hundred thousand pots of curd, milk and ghee to Civakan's wedding.
links.teaches: The herd chief's boast at his own daughter's giving is paid at Civakan's wedding instead, so the bond made by the recovered cattle carries from one marriage of the hero's circle to the next.

links.note: Civakan's teacher says those great in knowledge reach the path where hard deeds wear away; after the battle Civakan removes the battlefield's sin by an image of the Jina, a festival and gifts.
links.teaches: The epic gives the householder prince a route to clearing sin by rite and giving, beside the teacher's route of knowledge that wears deeds away, so the work holds two Jain answers to bad deeds at once and assigns them by station.

links.note: The Kural says it is not the spear but the ruler's unbent sceptre that gives victory; the epic says victory goes to the virtuous mind, and a betel leaf thrown by such a man becomes a spear.
links.teaches: The couplet ties victory to the justice of a king's rule, while the epic moves it into each fighter's heart and applies it to a war over a woman, where no sceptre is in question.

gains.a: the epic's moral of battle gains a political form, the rule that a just state wins, which its private quarrel over a bride lacks
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the side with fewer arms wins and the cause is put in character rather than in government

links.note: The Kural says a jackal can kill a war elephant when its feet sink in mud, so ground decides; the epic says a single lion kills a herd of elephants, so the nature of the fighter decides.
links.teaches: Both answer how the few beat the many, but the couplet credits the place of battle and the epic the strength of the one who fights, two incompatible accounts of the same reversal if each is taken as the cause.

gains.a: the epic's boast gains a rival explanation it does not consider, that its small band might have won by terrain or timing rather than by nature
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-image in which the elephant is the victim of a stronger beast, not of bad ground, which shows its claim is a choice of cause

links.note: In the Nedunalvadai the king walks the camp at midnight to look at the sword wounds of the warriors; in the epic the wounded are laid in ghee, have spearheads cut out, and are given purses and ornaments.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem shows care for the wounded as the king's sleepless looking, and the epic turns that care into a practice of treatment and payment, so the reader sees the duty to the wounded grow from presence into provision.

gains.a: the epic's list of treatments gains a source in the old ideal of the leader who goes himself to the wounded, which it leaves to friends and women
gains.b: the Sangam king's visit gains a picture of what was done for the wounded after he looked, which the poem does not tell

links.note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; the epic says the Tirthan's feet remove all the sins done, and has Civakan worship there after killing in battle.
links.teaches: The couplet's claim covers both good and bad deeds and asks only praise, while the epic narrows it to sins and stages it as a rite after a specific act of killing, showing how a general promise was put to work as expiation.

gains.a: the epic's rite gains a measure of how much less it claims than the couplet, which frees from good deeds too
gains.b: the couplet's abstract Lord gains a named object, the Jina's feet, and a concrete occasion, the sin of war

links.note: Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart and that those who wander the land without bathing in them do not destroy their deeds; Civakan takes the water of a jewelled conch at the Tirthan's feet as part of putting away his sin.
links.teaches: Read as part of the sin-clearing rite, the conch water is the outward tirtham Tirumular says cannot destroy deeds, so the pair sets an epic's confidence in rite against a Saiva yogi's insistence on the inward bath.

gains.a: the epic's ceremony gains a sharp critic, who would ask whether the water touched the heart
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a case from another faith of the outward practice he dismisses, done sincerely by a hero after war

source_issues: 807 line 3: கண்ணுட் டீயாற சுட்டு looks corrupt for கண்ணுள் தீயால் சுட்டு.
808 line 1: the word division is broken (சிலை கால்கு னிந்த for சிலை கால் குனிந்த).
811 line 1: தெழிக்ப் is a misprint for தெழிக்கப்.
812: printed with the number 811; read as 812 (the tool's numbering flag).
817 line 2: உழதசெஞ் reads as a misprint for உழுத செஞ்.
819 line 3: பதுமுகன் பாவை மார்பி னெய்க்கிழி is hard to construe; the line may be corrupt.
821 line 2: சேடங் கூலித் is doubtful; கூலித் gives no clear sense.
824 line 4: தாங்கொர்பால lacks the final pulli of the refrain ஒர்பால் found in 825 to 827.
Verses 805, 807, 808, 809, 812, 819: TSCII repairs of ோ் to ேர் (flagged by the tool); 814 to 817: stanzas printed in eight half-lines and joined.
